summary.text: A domestic shorthair cat aged 6.5 years was presented to a veterinary dentist with a 9-month history of anorexia and oral pain. Examination showed reddened, slightly raised plaques bilaterally on the caudal margins of the hard palate, and the cat also had multiple skin lesions.

Samples of a skin mass and the oral lesions were submitted for histology. The oral lesions were reported as papillomavirus-associated in situ carcinoma with Felis catus papillomavirus type 3 DNA, and the skin lesions were classified as cutaneous Bowenoid in situ carcinomas.

The cat was treated symptomatically for 18 months before being euthanatized because of increased oral pain and anorexia, and Table 1 lists the outcome as death due to oral pain 18 months after diagnosis.

summary.text: A domestic shorthair cat aged 8.5 years was presented to a veterinary dentist with ptyalism, decreased grooming and anorexia of 11 months duration. Stomatitis had initially been suspected by the referring veterinarian, but examination showed reddening and loss of lingual papillae on the dorsal tongue and a reddened erosive lesion caudally on the hard palate.

Samples from the tongue and hard palate were submitted for histology, which showed papillomavirus-associated oral in situ carcinoma with FcaPV3 DNA, vacuoles and basophilic cytoplasmic bodies. The cat was treated symptomatically.

At re-examination 13 months later the palatal and lingual lesions remained red and erosive with mild progression, and an additional sample was submitted. The re-sampled palatal lesion was nearly identical to the original biopsy, and Table 1 lists the cat as alive 13 months after diagnosis.

summary.text: A Persian cat aged 10 years had drooling and halitosis. Oral examination showed dental disease, a roughly circular area of loss of lingual papillae and reddening centrally on the dorsal tongue, and multiple slightly raised gray plaques ventrally and laterally on the tongue.

Three months later the tongue lesions persisted and multiple darkly pigmented skin lesions were found when the cat was clipped; samples from dorsal tongue, lateral tongue and skin were submitted for histology. Skin lesions were classified as cutaneous Bowenoid in situ carcinomas and the oral lesion contained FcaPV1 DNA.

Four months later two ulcerated, bleeding skin masses were excised and the tongue lesion was unchanged. Three months after that the cat developed hematuria and a palpable bladder mass, urothelial neoplasia was suspected, and the cat was euthanatized without necropsy; Table 1 gives death due to unrelated disease 7 months after diagnosis.

summary.text: A domestic shorthair cat aged 13 years initially developed ulcerative lesions on the nasal planum that were treated with cryotherapy without diagnostic testing. Two months later it developed signs of oral pain and a reddened, slightly raised 3 cm diameter area within the oropharynx.

The oral lesion had not resolved 6 months later and two samples were submitted for histology, which showed a papillomavirus-associated oral in situ carcinoma with FcaPV3 DNA. About 1 month after sampling the oral pain signs stopped and the lesions appeared less reddened.

Fourteen months later the cat developed skin lesions histologically diagnosed as cutaneous hemangiosarcoma. Metastases were detected and the cat was euthanatized without necropsy, with the oral lesion still present and not progressed; Table 1 gives death due to unrelated disease 14 months after diagnosis.

summary.text: A domestic shorthair cat aged 11 years had a lesion noticed on the dorsal surface of the tongue at a routine dental health check. It was initially treated with antibiotics, but the lesion rapidly increased in size over the following 2 months.

The lesion was then a well-demarcated, 2 cm diameter, reddened area with loss of lingual papillae rostrally on the left side of the dorsal tongue, and the cat was drooling and grooming less frequently. It was treated symptomatically for 24 months, during which the lesions neither progressed nor resolved.

The cat was presented at a veterinary dentistry specialty practice and a sample was taken for histology, which showed a papillomavirus-associated oral in situ carcinoma with FcaPV3 DNA. The cat is alive 6 months after diagnosis, with no anorexia but drooling of blood-tinged saliva and reluctance to groom.

caption_evidence.quote:
Figure 2.
Photomicrographs of papillomavirus-associated oral in situ carcinomas in cats. Hematoxylin and eosin. (a) Case 4, dorsal tongue. The epithelium is irregularly thickened with rounded trabeculae extending into the underlying lamina propria. There is no infiltration through the basement membrane. (b) Case 1, lower lip. As is seen in cutaneous Bowenoid in situ carcinomas, the basal cells are crowded and vertically elongated. Keratinized cells are present within deeper layers of the epithelium (black arrow), and cells with basophilic elongated perinuclear cytoplasmic bodies are visible (white arrow). (c) Case 3, dorsal tongue. The thickened epithelium lacks regular organization, and a prominent layer of lymphocytic inflammation forms a band within the underlying lamina propria. (d) Case 4, dorsal tongue. Clear vacuoles are prominent within the epithelial cells (black arrows). In addition, cells containing increased quantities of blue-gray cytoplasm are visible superficially within the thickened epithelium (white arrows). (e) Case 4, palate. Numerous elongated basophilic cytoplasmic bodies are visible surrounding the nuclei within the affected epithelium. Felis catus papillomavirus (FcaPV) 3 DNA was amplified from this lesion. (f) Case 5, lateral tongue margin. The sample contains large brick-like cytoplasmic bodies that are surrounded by a clear halo. Compared to the other lesions, the thickening of the epithelium appears more orderly with little dysplasia. This lesion contains FcaPV1 DNA. Inset. Case 3, dorsal tongue. Epithelial cells show intense diffuse nuclear and cytoplasmic p16^(CDKN2A) protein immunolabeling. p16^(CDKN2A) immunohistochemistry.

article_limitations: Veterinary case series of 7 cats; each cat is a separate roster patient numbered by the Table 1 row order. Breed is kept only in case context because the demographics schema has no breed attribute.

Series-level and unlabelled sentences were not copied to individual cats: the abstract and discussion counts, outcome summaries, "most of the cats" statements, the unlabelled histology sentences that follow the all-7 sentence (basal-cell crowding, keratinized cells, brick-like bodies and blue-gray cytoplasm in the results paragraph), and the FcaPV1 versus FcaPV3 comparison paragraph.
Case 7 sex conflict: Table 1 gives MN (male neutered) while the case narrative uses the pronoun She; both are recorded as review-only source conflicts and no sex is accepted for case 7.

Case 6 outcome timing: Table 1 gives death 14 months after diagnosis, while the text places the hemangiosarcoma skin lesions 14 months after a follow-up that was about 1 month after sampling; recorded as an ambiguity.
Treatments given as "treated symptomatically" or "treated for stomatitis" are recorded as unspecified treatments because the source names no drug or procedure.
Table 1 image and the three figure rows are inspected in a separate visual submission; the caption-layer annotation keeps visual_status not_inspected.
Oncology biomarker items for p16 immunolabeling and PV DNA were not created; those results are recorded as observations.
"none of the cats had obvious signs of immunosuppression or a history of immunosuppressive therapy" names the 7 cats of the series and is recorded for each cat.
Unsampled or mildly dysplastic second oral sites (case 3 ventral tongue, case 5 lateral tongue edges) are recorded as oral lesions, not as diagnosed in situ carcinomas.
